evidence.quote: Eighteen attempted suicide patients in a specialized ward for suicidal patients were interviewed about their feelings, thoughts, and reactions during the hospitalization. In a content analysis of the data, it was found that shame reactions were spontaneously described by many of the respondents. The data also indicated that shame may have played an important role in the attempted suicide patients' experiences of the care received. For this reason, shame reactions were chosen as the focus of a separate study, and are reported in this article. The 13 interviews containing shame expressions were selected and analysed further with respect to shame reactions.

Twenty-one consecutively admitted Swedish-speaking attempted suicide patients in a specialized psychiatric ward for suicidal patients were asked to participate in an interview study about their experiences of the psychiatric care provided. Eighteen patients, six women and 12 men aged 18–53, agreed to participate in the interview study.
Shame reactions were spontaneously described by 13 of 18 patients interviewed in a qualitative study investigating experiences of care following a suicide attempt.
Eighteen attempted suicide patients in a specialized ward for suicidal patients were interviewed about their feelings, thoughts, and reactions during the hospitalization.

[page/6/Text/4] The respondents in the study were consecutively admitted attempted suicide patients, who agreed to participate in the study. ... In this study, a majority of the respondents were male.

The aim of the original interview data collection was to elucidate the attempted suicide patients' experiences of receiving specialized inpatient psychiatric care. The findings from the content analysis of the interviews are reported elsewhere (11). The aim of the present study was to extract and analyse the interview data concerning experiences of shame, which were reported spontaneously by a majority of the respondents in the interview study.

evidence.section_title: Descriptions of shame used as inclusion criteria for the shame analysis
evidence.quote: [/page/1/Text/11] Respondents from the interview study, who were interpreted by the authors as describing shame reactions, were chosen for the present shame study.

Shame reactions often occurred in conjunction with the suicide attempt. Feelings of shame were accompanied by impulses to hide or flee, i.e., fear of seeking help or impulses to leave the hospital. The attempted suicide patients often experienced the initial encounter at the hospital as difficult. Having attempted suicide and survived was often perceived as yet another failure, in addition to the problems leading to the attempt. The attempted suicide patients were sensitive to the attitudes and behaviours of the personnel. Experiencing the personnel as kind, respectful, and nonjudgemental seemed to contribute to a relief from shame for some patients. Some respondents expressed that a tolerant and flexible atmosphere in the psychiatric ward, with low demands on the attempted suicide patient, helped them accept treatment and made them feel less ashamed for not living up to the expectations of everyday life. On the other hand, feeling too exposed to others or experiencing negative attitudes from the personnel seemed to contribute to an exacerbation of shame for some patients.

All respondents described that they had felt distress after the suicide attempt and that the initial encounter at the hospital was emotionally difficult. The respondents often experienced shame immediately after the suicide attempt and during the first encounters with the hospital personnel. Several patients described that their feelings of shame were alleviated, diminished, or were made more bearable when they were treated with kindness and respect. The feelings of shame were replaced by feelings of relief that they had received help.

evidence.section_title: Aspects of care that were associated with feelings of shame
evidence.quote: Respondents experienced that different aspects of care alleviated their feelings of shame. For many respondents, being treated with kindness and respect during the first encounters at the hospital alleviated their initial shame reaction after the suicide attempt and helped them make the decision to agree to being admitted into the psychiatric clinic. Respondents described that their feelings of shame were exacerbated when they felt that they had exposed themselves too much and when they experienced the personnel as unsympathetic, disrespectful, authoritative, and punishing.

Many respondents described feelings of shame and sensitivity to the attitudes of the personnel at the time of admission to the hospital. Respondents' feelings of shame were sometimes alleviated or exacerbated during interaction with the hospital personnel. ... [page/6/Text/10] Shame reactions were common and threatened to restrain the patients from accepting admittance to hospital and from expressing their needs. Shame also made them sensitive to exposure situations and negative attitudes from the personnel. At the same time, experiencing the personnel as kind and respectful helped these patients to accept care and was perceived as alleviating feelings of shame.
